nature-eco-505.title: What aquatic ecosystems do for us
nature-eco-505.text: A river or lake partly cleans itself. Microorganisms, plankton, plants, invertebrates and fish break down organic matter and filter the water as they feed and grow. That is one of the functions of aquatic ecosystems: the environmental and human services they provide. They recycle nutrients, purify water, reduce floods, refill underground water and provide wildlife habitat. They also give people places to play. Water-based recreation is very important to tourism, especially on coasts. And they carry meaning beyond money, serving religious and educational uses, from pilgrimage to the Jordan River to the ecological study of lakes.

nature-eco-502.title: Freshwater ecosystems: rich life in scarce water
nature-eco-502.text: Swamps, deltas and rivers make up just 1% of Earth's surface, yet freshwater ecosystems hold 41% of the world's known fish species. A freshwater ecosystem is an aquatic ecosystem of low-salt water: lakes, ponds, rivers, streams, springs, bogs and wetlands. That sets it apart from the sea, whose water is much saltier. The three basic types are lentic (still water such as ponds and lakes), lotic (flowing water such as rivers) and wetlands. Still and flowing water are the two classic forms. Scientists also classify freshwater habitats by temperature, light penetration, nutrients and vegetation. Land-based fresh waters produce about 1.5% of global net primary production, the plant growth left after plants meet their own energy needs. Many freshwater organisms cannot tolerate salt, and irrigation water can pick up harmful levels of it. Five broad threats stand out: overexploitation, water pollution, changed water flows, habitat destruction and invasive species.

nature-eco-499.title: Marine ecosystems: the salty majority of the planet
nature-eco-499.text: Marine waters cover more than 70% of Earth's surface and hold more than 97% of its water and 90% of its habitable space. A marine ecosystem is a salty-water aquatic ecosystem, the largest kind on Earth. Seawater averages a salinity, or saltiness, of 35 parts per thousand, though it varies between ecosystems. Scientists divide the sea into zones by depth and distance from shore, such as the open oceanic zone and the benthic zone on the seabed. The range is vast. Near the coast it includes reefs built by corals, mangroves, underwater meadows of sea plants, forests of giant seaweed, estuaries, lagoons and tidal marshes. Farther out lie the open ocean surface and the dark depths. Open-water systems regulate the global climate, feed the water cycle, maintain biodiversity, and provide food, energy, recreation and tourism. Marine systems also support billions of dollars' worth of fishing, fish farming, offshore oil and gas, and shipping. Coastal fishing from mangroves and reefs alone is estimated to be worth at least $34 billion per year.

nature-eco-530.title: Estuaries: where rivers meet the sea
nature-eco-530.text: Of the thirty-two largest cities in the early 1990s, twenty-two stood on estuaries. An estuary is a partly enclosed coastal water body where river or stream freshwater mixes with seawater to form brackish water. It is an ecotone, a transition zone where two environments overlap, in this case river and sea. Tides, waves and salt water from the sea combine with river flow and sediment to shape it. Most estuaries are young. They formed in the Holocene, when rising seas flooded river valleys about 10,000–12,000 years ago. The mixing of fresh and salt water makes them nutrient-rich and among the most productive natural habitats in the world. It also makes life hard. Salinity ranges from near zero at the river's tidal limit to 3.4% at the mouth, and it shifts with tides and seasons.

nature-eco-554.title: The pelagic zone: life in the open ocean
nature-eco-554.text: About 80% of ocean carbon fixation, the capture of carbon into living matter, happens in the open ocean, which covers more than 90% of the ocean area. Its water column is the pelagic zone: the open ocean away from the shore and the seabed. Moving down it, pressure rises, temperature and light fall, and salinity, oxygen and nutrients change. The whole system rests on phytoplankton, which need sunlight and so live in the upper sunlit layer. Below that layer biodiversity drops sharply, as oxygen, food and light dwindle and pressure and cold increase. The fish of the open sea are often migratory forage fish, small schooling species such as herring and anchovies, along with the tuna and sharks that follow them.

nature-eco-516.title: The deep sea: Earth's least explored biome
nature-eco-516.text: In 1960 the bathyscaphe Trieste, a deep-diving vessel, reached the bottom of the Mariana Trench at 10,911 m, the deepest known spot in any ocean. The deep sea is the part of the ocean below about 200 m (660 ft), where light fades and the continental shelf gives way to the slope. It is cold, dark and under crushing pressure, and it is the least explored biome on Earth. Pressure rises about 1 atmosphere every 10 meters, reaching more than 1,000 atmospheres in places. No other habitat on Earth is so constant: its temperature barely changes over long periods, and salinity stays at about 35 parts per thousand throughout. Without light there is no photosynthesis. Life depends on food sinking from above or on chemical energy at vents in the seafloor. Deep-sea fish tend to be small, with slow metabolisms, and many use bioluminescence, light made by their own bodies, to hide their silhouettes.

nature-eco-531.title: Estuaries as nurseries, filters and buffers
nature-eco-531.text: Commercial fishing depends on estuaries for approximately 68 percent of its catch by value. That makes the benefits estuaries give people and nature, from fish nurseries and clean water to storm protection, unusually easy to see in money. Estuaries are nurseries for young fish and shellfish. They sustain mangroves, underwater sea plants and tidal marshes, which in turn support fishing. Estuary wetlands filter sediment, nutrients and pollutants from runoff coming off the land, improving water quality. Marsh grasses hold shorelines in place, buffering storms and sea-level rise and protecting roads and buildings. Estuaries also serve as migration corridors for fish and habitat for migratory birds, which draw nature tourists.

nature-eco-470.title: Grassland carbon: stored out of sight
nature-eco-470.text: Soil carbon makes up about 81% of all carbon in grassland ecosystems. Grasslands store carbon mostly underground, in their deep roots and the soil, rather than in above-ground plants. There is a good reason. Carbon above ground does not last long, because grazing, fire and plants dying back keep removing it. Below ground it can stay put. Stocks are highest where rainfall is heaviest and fall as temperatures rise. Human activity has drained this store. Soil disturbance, degradation, fire and erosion have caused large carbon losses, though good management can reverse them. How big the opportunity is remains unsettled. Researchers have not agreed on how much carbon grasslands can store, partly because measurement methods differ and data are limited. Until they do, estimates of grassland carbon should be read as uncertain.

nature-eco-471.title: Grassland degradation: the quiet loss of open land
nature-eco-471.text: Global losses from grassland degradation are estimated at over $7 billion per year. Grassland degradation is the loss or decline of grasslands, driven mainly by farming, mining and other human uses of land. Most of the world's grasslands have been converted to fields of corn, wheat and other crops. Of 70 grassland ecoregions, regions with distinct natural communities, 21 are less than 20% intact and only 14 keep at least 60%; 47 have declined since 2000. Grasslands are vulnerable for three reasons: they are misclassified, poorly protected and cultivated. Climate change adds a new pressure. As many grasslands become warmer and drier, non-native grasses are expected to outperform native ones.

nature-eco-474.title: Grassland restoration: bringing back the open range
nature-eco-474.text: Only seven large, continuous grassland regions remain relatively intact on Earth. Grassland restoration aims to bring back degraded grasslands, though knowledge of the options is still limited. The toolkit draws on the forces that kept grasslands open in the first place. It includes prescribed fire, set deliberately under control, managing livestock and wild grazers, cutting trees and shrubs, controlling invasive species and reseeding native plants. Costs vary widely, and cost data are scarce. Success needs more than fieldwork: policy recognition, standard indicators of degradation, research and data sharing. The UN General Assembly proclaimed 2021–2030 the UN Decade on Restoration, led by UNEP and the FAO.

nature-eco-494.title: How wetlands release methane and nitrous oxide
nature-eco-494.text: Wetlands are the world's largest natural source of atmospheric methane, supplying roughly 20–30% of it, about 161 Tg a year on average. That makes them a major climate concern. Wetland greenhouse gas emissions are the release of these warming gases, chiefly methane and nitrous oxide, from wetland soils and plants. The cause is a shortage of oxygen. In waterlogged soils, microbes use up oxygen faster than it can seep in. That suits methane-making microbes, which live by anaerobic respiration, breaking down food without oxygen. Warmer, more oxygen-starved soils rich in organic matter produce methane more efficiently. Some wetlands also emit nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas with 300 times the warming potential of carbon dioxide. Excess nutrients, mostly from human sources, sharply increase its release. There is another side. Wetlands can also act as sinks: 14.5% of the world's soil carbon lies in wetlands, which cover 5.5% of land. Other estimates in the same sources put the share higher, at 20–30% of soil carbon on 5–8% of land.

nature-eco-477.title: Peatland carbon: more than half the air's store
nature-eco-477.text: Peatlands cover only 3% of land, yet they hold between 500 and 700 billion tonnes of carbon, over half the amount in the atmosphere. They store so much because plants keep adding dead matter faster than it can decompose in the waterlogged ground. Peatlands still take up 0.37 gigatons of CO2 a year. Their climate balance is subtle. Natural mires, peatlands still forming peat, are a small CO2 sink, but most also emit methane and nitrous oxide. Over millennia, though, peatlands have had a net cooling effect on the atmosphere. The main control is the water table, the level below which the ground is saturated. When it drops, oxygen reaches the peat, and decomposition releases more CO2. Keeping peat wet is what keeps its carbon locked away.

nature-eco-478.title: Draining peatlands: turning a sink into a source
nature-eco-478.text: Peatlands cover only 3% of land, but their degradation produces 7% of all CO2 emissions. Most of that damage starts with a ditch. People drain peatlands to lower the water table for farming and timber, which turns them from carbon sinks into carbon sources. Farming and timber growing, the main human uses, cover around a quarter of global peatland area. Drainage lets oxygen into the peat. Microbes can then decompose it, releasing carbon dioxide and methane that had been locked away for centuries. Degraded peatlands account for 5-10% of global carbon emissions from human activities. The damage goes beyond carbon. Extreme drying can shift a mire, a living peat-forming wetland, into barren land with less biodiversity.

nature-nbs-127.title: Peatland restoration: blocking the ditches
nature-nbs-127.text: Peatlands cover 400 million hectares, 3% of Earth's land surface, and many have been drained for peat cutting, farmland and timber. Drainage damaged their habitats, water flow, nutrient flows and carbon balance. Peatland restoration usually blocks drainage channels to rewet the peat and lets native vegetation recover. Rewetting cuts carbon release in the short term, and new plant growth eventually restarts peat formation. The payoff is large. Drained peatlands release large amounts of greenhouse gases, while an intact one stores carbon and purifies water, filtering and holding metals and other toxins for long periods. The IPCC, the UN's climate science panel, weighed in with its Sixth Assessment Report. It says conserving and restoring wetlands and peatlands has large economic potential to cut emissions, with benefits for adaptation and biodiversity. The {{ref:nature-gov-015}} names peatlands as key ecosystems to protect, and wetlands are also covered by the 1971 {{ref:nature-gov-051}}. The Global Peatlands Initiative, formed in 2016, works to keep peatland carbon in the ground.

nature-eco-511.title: What bogs give: carbon, water and berries
nature-eco-511.text: The Yangtze, one of Asia's great rivers, rises in a peatland, the Ruoergai. Peat bogs store fresh water near the headwaters of large rivers, one of the benefits intact bogs give people along with carbon storage, food and recreation. The carbon role cuts both ways. Left undisturbed, bogs remain a carbon sink. If their peat decays, the carbon escapes as carbon dioxide and adds to global warming. The peatlands of the former Soviet Union were calculated to remove 52 Tg of carbon per year from the atmosphere. Rewetting drained peatlands may be among the most cost-effective ways to slow climate change. Bogs also feed people: wild blueberries, cranberries, cloudberries and lingonberries are harvested from them, and they draw visitors who come for wildlife and hunting.

nature-eco-536.title: Fens: peatlands fed by groundwater
nature-eco-536.text: A fen is a peat-building wetland fed by mineral-rich water from the ground or the surface. Bogs and fens together are called mires. Their water supply gives them more minerals and a more basic, less acidic pH than bogs. Fens store large amounts of carbon as peat, and destroying the peat layer can release it. Whether fens are net absorbers or emitters of greenhouse gases is still disputed, because their waterlogged soils produce methane. They can also clean nitrogen-rich farm runoff. Conversion to farmland has destroyed many, especially in Europe and North America, and restoration often blocks drains to bring the water back.

nature-eco-513.title: Boreal ecosystems: the subarctic belt of the north
nature-eco-513.text: Boreal soils hold about 338 Pg of carbon, comparable to the carbon in all the living matter of tropical ecosystems. A petagram (Pg) is a billion tonnes. A boreal ecosystem is a subarctic ecosystem of the Northern Hemisphere, roughly between 50° and 70°N, commonly called taiga. It spans parts of North America, Europe and Asia. Its plants range from black and white spruce to willows, wildflowers and alders, and caribou move in during winter to eat lichen. Boreal systems are less diverse than tropical ones but still hold a variety of species. Disturbance keeps them cycling. Wildfires, floods, mudslides and insect outbreaks clear ground and drive secondary succession, the regrowth of plant communities on disturbed land. Boreal ecosystems are among those most vulnerable to climate change.

nature-eco-446.title: Wetland products: rice, fish and fuelwood
nature-eco-446.text: Rice, a wetland crop, supplies one fifth of all calories eaten worldwide. Wetlands naturally produce plants, fish and other goods that people harvest for their own use and for sale. Many fish spend all or part of their lives in wetlands, and fish are the main protein source for about one billion people. Mangroves supply fuelwood, salt, fodder, traditional medicines, textile fibres, dyes and tannins. In one region alone, the Lower Mekong basin, wetlands support over 55 million people.

nature-eco-444.title: How wetlands clean water
nature-eco-444.text: Wetlands clean water by taking up nutrients and trapping sediment and the pollutants attached to it. Their plants slow the water so that sediment settles and is trapped, along with any heavy metals it carries. This filtering is efficient, but every wetland has a limit. Too much fertilizer washing off fields, or too much sewage, tips it into eutrophication, the overgrowth of algae fed by excess nutrients. Too much sediment is also harmful. Heavy loads washing down from cleared forests upstream can shrink wetlands and cause sharp biodiversity loss.

nature-eco-445.title: Wetlands that treat a city's sewage
nature-eco-445.text: The East Kolkata Wetlands in India cover 125 square kilometres and treat the city's sewage, and the nutrients in that waste feed fish farms and crops. Natural wetlands and specially built ones ({{ref:nature-nbs-158}}) can be used to treat sewage and other wastewater. Built wetlands use plants, soil and organisms to remove suspended solids, organic matter, nitrogen, phosphorus and disease-causing germs. In cities they do more than clean water. They also reduce floods, store carbon and provide wildlife habitat.

nature-eco-561.title: Temperate forests: the woods where people settled
nature-eco-561.text: Temperate forests grow where much of humanity lives, and they have paid for it. A temperate forest is a forest of the temperate zone, lying between the tropical and boreal regions. It spans latitudes of about 25 to 50 degrees in both hemispheres and includes deciduous, coniferous, mixed and rainforest types. It is the second largest forest biome, with 25% of the world's forest area, behind the boreal forest's roughly 33%. These forests were long cleared for cities and farming, and they still suffer logging, mining, pollution and habitat loss. Most temperate rainforests outside protected land have been cut down.

nature-eco-437.title: Urban ecosystems: the city as a habitat
nature-eco-437.text: Cities hold more than half of the world's population, and their numbers are expected to keep growing. An urban ecosystem is the ecosystem of a city, town or industrial area: a complex patchwork of buildings, roads, parks and gardens created and maintained by people. It cannot feed itself. Urban ecosystems depend on large imports of water, nutrients, food and other resources. Dense human populations interacting with many kinds of patches produce complex feedbacks among the parts of the system. Social-ecology treats a city as part of a wider system linking its people with the surrounding landscapes. Cities offer jobs, healthcare and education, but urban growth worsens pollution and the loss of green space and biodiversity. Studying urban ecosystems has led to proposals for city design that does less harm to surrounding environments.

nature-eco-411.title: How mangroves survive salt and mud
nature-eco-411.text: Some mangroves breathe through straws. Their pneumatophores are root-like tubes that stick up out of the mud so the plant can get air. Mangroves have evolved special roots, leaves and seeds that let them cope with salty water, waterlogged mud and tides. Red mangrove roots are coated with suberin, a waxy substance, and act as a filter that keeps most sodium salts out. Many mangroves are viviparous: their seeds sprout while still on the parent tree, then drop as floating seedlings that water can carry far away. Different species tolerate water from brackish, through seawater at 3 to 4% salinity, up to 9% salinity.

nature-eco-414.title: Mangrove carbon: blue carbon in wood and mud
nature-eco-414.text: Mangroves worldwide stored 4.19 Gt of carbon in 2012. Mangroves take up carbon and lock it away in their wood and sediments. That makes them an important store of coastal carbon, part of what is called {{ref:nature-nbs-034}}. They are among the most carbon-rich biomes and account for 11% of the carbon that flows from land into the oceans. Fallen mangrove material can turn into peat, with help from termites that work litter and wood into their nests, which get buried. Losses undo the store: two percent of mangrove carbon was lost between 2000 and 2012, equal to at most 0.316996250 Gt of carbon dioxide emissions.

nature-eco-413.title: Mangroves as nurseries for young fish
nature-eco-413.text: Lemon sharks give birth in mangrove creeks, where pups find cover and practise hunting with few predators around. The tangle of mangrove roots forms a sheltered underwater habitat where young fish and other sea animals grow up. The submerged roots carry algae, barnacles, oysters and sponges, while shrimps and mud lobsters live in the muddy bottom. This nursery has a market value. Mangroves in Vietnam, Thailand, the Philippines and India support several commercially important fish and crustacean species.

nature-eco-417.title: What forests do for the planet and for people
nature-eco-417.text: Forests host 80% of all land-dwelling organisms. They provide many benefits to the planet and to people, from oxygen and carbon storage to water regulation, soil protection, habitat and products. They produce about 28% of Earth's oxygen and act as crucial carbon sinks. Trees store large amounts of water and help regulate underground water, evaporation and rain and snow patterns. Some researchers describe a 'biotic pump', in which forests help drive the water cycle by drawing moisture in from the ocean. Forests also hold the ground together. Without them, erosion and sediment get worse, and removing or compacting leaf litter worsens erosion and flooding. About 399 million ha of forest are set aside mainly to protect soil and water, 119 million ha more than in 1990. People also rely directly on forests for fuel and wood products; the boreal forest alone supplies much lumber and paper.

nature-eco-418.title: What threatens the world's forests
nature-eco-418.text: Forests are threatened mainly by clearing for timber, land, mining, cities and farming, and by climate change. Deforestation removes large areas for timber and land development. Clearing also breaks the forest that remains into smaller patches, making it harder for forest species to find food, shelter and mates, which cuts biodiversity. Mining clears native forest, and its logging and smelting cause soil erosion and acidification that slow recovery. Farming turns forest into fields and single-crop plantations and brings fertilizers and pesticides that harm the soil. Urbanization splits habitats with roads, cities and infrastructure, displacing wildlife. On top of all this, climate change harms forests through wildfires, droughts, soil erosion and heat stress.
